COMPREHENSIVE NEEDS ASSESSMENT

Understand what your school needs

Review the four data types, use the school starting evidence, and add the local evidence only your school knows.

0 of 4 complete

Four Types of Data

Select a data type to begin or continue your review.

Data Type

Make meaning

What is the evidence telling us?

Capture the pattern—not a list of numbers. Name who is most affected when the evidence shows a meaningful difference.

Go deeper

Review the CNA domain(s)

Use the domains below only after you have oriented to the evidence for this data type.

Explore

Bring the four data types together.
Before naming a need, look for patterns that converge across demographic, perception, process, and outcome evidence. A priority should not come from one isolated result.
Narrow

Determine School Needs

Do not carry every concern forward. Keep only patterns with meaningful evidence and scholar impact.

Stronger need statement: “Grade 6 multilingual learners are showing lower reading growth across NWEA, classroom assessments, and scholar work” is more useful than “Reading scores are low.”
Investigate

Understand Why the Need Exists

Separate the outcome from the likely contributing condition. Focus on conditions the school or district can influence.

Root-cause test: A useful cause explains the pattern, is supported by evidence, and is influenceable. Avoid restating the problem or blaming scholars or families.
Decide

Set Priorities

Select 2–4 needs. Use four tests: Is the pattern persistent? Is scholar impact meaningful? Do we understand enough about why it is happening? Would addressing it materially improve outcomes?

Before selecting a priority: the domain should be reviewed using at least two evidence types. The final CNA should normally carry only the few needs the school is prepared to address and monitor.
CONNECT

Connect the Need to the Plan

Before choosing or funding a strategy, make the logic explicit. This follows the If → Then → So That structure used in the School Index planning templates.

Keep this practical: The school has already identified the need and likely root cause. This step checks whether the proposed action actually addresses that cause and names the result the school expects to see.
IF we...implement the strategy or activity that addresses the root cause
THEN we expect...the condition connected to the priority need to improve
SO THAT...scholars experience a measurable improvement in outcomes
Synthesize

SMART CONNECTIONS

Connect CNA Priorities to the Title I Plan

The system reviews each selected CNA priority, its domain, affected scholars, gap, and root cause, then identifies the Title I requirements that should carry that need forward.

How this works: Connections are recommendations, not automatic compliance decisions. The school confirms which connections are relevant and completes the school-specific details required in each section.
Connections update automatically when CNA priorities change.

MODEL EXAMPLE

A completed CNA — in five moves

Illustrative example — not actual school results

Sample GRPS Middle School | 2026–27

Use this as a quick model. Move through one step at a time; open details only if you want to see the evidence behind the example.

STEP 1 — EVIDENCE

What did the team notice?

1. Demographic41% chronic absence; highest in grades 7–8 and among scholars with high mobility.
2. Outcome / Scholar LearningReading and written-response weaknesses repeat across NWEA, M-STEP ELA, and course performance.
3. ProcessEarly warning signs are identified, but barrier documentation and follow-through vary by team.
4. PerceptionRelationships are a strength, while belonging and communication are less consistent in grade 8.
What the four types tell us togetherAttendance is limiting access to instruction, and inconsistent response systems are contributing to the pattern.

Takeaway: The CNA does not treat the four data types as four separate reports. It uses them together to identify a school need.

STEP 2 — NEED

Turn the pattern into a school need.

Built from Demographic + Process + Perception evidence
Gap41% chronic absence and inconsistent follow-through after early warning signs.
NeedA reliable early-warning and barrier-response system that acts before absence becomes chronic.

Takeaway: The need describes what must improve—not the program the school plans to buy or implement.

STEP 3 — WHY

Identify the root cause the school can influence.

Confirmed through Process + Perception evidence
Root causeOwnership, barrier documentation, and follow-up expectations are not consistently defined.

Takeaway: Root cause comes after the need so the team does not jump straight to a solution.

What evidence would confirm this?

Attendance-team records, contact logs, staff interviews, family feedback, and intervention documentation.

STEP 4 — PRIORITY

Only the highest-leverage need moves forward.

Priority reflects the pattern across all four data types
Priority: Early Attendance & Belonging Response

Focus the work on early warning, relationship-based outreach, barrier identification, and matched support.

Takeaway: A strong CNA narrows the work. It does not produce a long list of disconnected initiatives.

STEP 5 — PLAN

Connect the priority to the strategy and expected result.

The plan is anchored to the need identified through the four-data-type review
IF we…use early warning data and relationship-based outreach to identify barriers quickly,
THEN…teams will respond earlier and more consistently,
SO THAT…fewer scholars move into chronic absence and more scholars have consistent access to instruction.

That is the full CNA story: Evidence → Need → Root Cause → Priority → Plan.

Want the detailed model?

Full written example

Four-type evidence review: Demographic data show concentrated chronic absence and mobility patterns. Outcome / scholar learning data show recurring literacy weaknesses. Process data show inconsistent follow-through after early warning signs. Perception data show strong relationships overall but weaker belonging and communication in grade 8. Together, these data point to an access-and-response need rather than four disconnected problems.

Need: The school needs a reliable early attendance and barrier-response system and more consistent literacy instruction and progress monitoring.

Root cause: Ownership, follow-up expectations, instructional response, and progress-monitoring routines are not consistently defined or implemented.

Priorities: Early Attendance & Belonging Response and Consistent Literacy Instruction & Intervention.
